reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: A cause of chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction from primary degeneration of gastrointestinal smooth muscle
Presents with recurrent episodes of obstruction (distension, vomiting, pain, constipation) in the absence of a mechanical lesion
Characteristic findings include megaduodenum, dilated bowel loops, and often a dilated bladder (megacystis) reflecting smooth-muscle involvement beyond the gut
Can be familial (frequently autosomal dominant) or sporadic, and may involve the whole gut as well as urinary tract smooth muscle
Contrast studies and imaging show dilated, poorly contracting segments and delayed transit without an obstructing lesion
Full-thickness intestinal biopsy shows smooth-muscle degeneration, vacuolation, and fibrosis, distinguishing myopathic from neuropathic pseudo-obstruction
Management is supportive with nutritional support, prokinetic and symptom-directed measures, and treatment of bacterial overgrowth, avoiding unnecessary surgery
reference.pathophysiology: Hollow visceral myopathy is a primary disorder of gastrointestinal (and often urinary tract) smooth muscle, in which degeneration, vacuolar change, and replacement fibrosis of the muscle layers impair contractile function. The weakened, poorly contracting muscle cannot generate effective peristalsis, so luminal contents stagnate and the bowel dilates, producing the clinical picture of pseudo-obstruction with megaduodenum and megacystis despite a patent lumen. Stasis promotes small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth and malabsorption, compounding malnutrition.
additionalDifferentials: Systemic sclerosis and other connective-tissue disease affecting gut muscle
Intestinal neuronal dysplasia and other dysganglionoses
Severe diabetic or paraneoplastic gastrointestinal dysmotility
additionalInvestigations: Abdominal radiography and contrast studies showing dilated, non-obstructed bowel and delayed transit
Cross-sectional imaging to exclude a mechanical cause and assess bladder and bowel calibre
Full-thickness intestinal biopsy with histology and immunohistochemistry of the muscle layers
Nutritional assessment and testing for bacterial overgrowth
redFlags: Acute severe distension with concern for perforation or ischaemia
Sepsis from bacterial overgrowth, translocation, or line infection during parenteral nutrition
Severe malnutrition and dependence on parenteral support
Urinary retention or upper tract dilatation from bladder involvement
reference.prognosis: The course is typically chronic and progressive, with morbidity from malnutrition, dependence on parenteral nutrition, and recurrent pseudo-obstructive episodes; prognosis depends on the extent of gut involvement and complications of long-term nutritional support.
pitfalls: Performing repeated laparotomies for presumed mechanical obstruction that is actually pseudo-obstruction
Failing to obtain full-thickness biopsy to distinguish myopathic from neuropathic disease
Overlooking urinary tract involvement (megacystis) as part of the same disorder
Neglecting bacterial overgrowth and nutritional deficiencies as sources of morbidity
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Prioritise nutritional support with small frequent low-residue feeds, enteral feeding where tolerated, and parenteral nutrition when intestinal failure supervenes
Treat small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth with cyclical antibiotics to reduce malabsorption and bloating
Manage pseudo-obstructive episodes with bowel rest, nasogastric or intestinal decompression, and fluid and electrolyte correction while avoiding unnecessary laparotomy
Trial prokinetic agents cautiously given limited efficacy in myopathic disease, and avoid opioids and other gut-slowing drugs
Address concurrent urinary tract smooth-muscle involvement with urology, using intermittent catheterisation for incomplete bladder emptying
Monitor for complications of long-term parenteral nutrition, including catheter sepsis, venous thrombosis and intestinal-failure-associated liver disease
Refer to a specialist intestinal-failure and gut-motility centre and consider intestinal transplantation in refractory intestinal failure
Offer genetic counselling and family assessment where an autosomal dominant familial form is identified
